exam: A 35‑year‑old man with progressive dysphagia to solids then liquids and regurgitation – what is the next best investigation? — Barium swallow to look for a bird‑beak; if unavailable, consider endoscopy.
A patient with heartburn and nocturnal cough – how do you differentiate GERD from asthma? — Look for relief with antacids and absence of wheeze; consider trial of PPI.
A child with fever, odynophagia, and white plaques on the esophageal mucosa – what is the likely pathogen and treatment? — Candida; treat with fluconazole.
A 50‑year‑old HIV‑positive patient presents with odynophagia and fever – what viral cause should you suspect and what drug is first line? — CMV; ganciclovir.
A patient with severe chest pain after a meal and vomiting – what life‑threatening complication must you rule out? — Esophageal perforation; urgent imaging and surgical consult.
A patient with dysphagia and weight loss but normal endoscopy – what further test can clarify the diagnosis? — Esophageal manometry to assess motility.
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Esophageal disease ranges from reflux to motility disorders and infections. Clinical reasoning focuses on history, exam, and pragmatic investigations, with treatment tailored to local resources.

b: History of dysphagia, regurgitation, chest pain, weight loss
sections.p: Esophageal disease encompasses reflux, motility disorders, structural lesions, and infections. Diagnosis starts with a focused history and physical, then uses the most available investigations.

t.b: Assesses structural abnormalities and motility; a corkscrew or bird‑beak appearance suggests achalasia.
Direct visualization of mucosal lesions, strictures, or ulceration; essential when bleeding or severe dysphagia is present.
Gold standard for motility disorders; identifies failed LES relaxation in achalasia.
Detects hypoxia from aspiration or severe reflux.

b: Achalasia: I (normal LES pressure, incomplete relaxation), II (pan‑esophageal pressurisation), III (spastic)
sections.p: Staging guides management. GERD is staged by symptom frequency and complications; achalasia is staged by Chicago classification (I‑III).

b: Herbal remedies: caustic alkalis causing strictures
sections.p: In low‑resource settings, infections and nutritional deficiencies are common. Lifestyle and herbal remedies also contribute.

b: Odynophagia, fever, malaise, white plaques on mucosa
sections.p: Symptoms guide the differential. Reflux presents with heartburn; achalasia with progressive dysphagia and regurgitation; infections with odynophagia and fever.

b: Use pulse oximetry and chest X‑ray for suspected aspiration or perforation.
sections.p: Choose tests based on availability and clinical urgency.

sections.p: Differential diagnosis includes cardiac pain, esophageal cancer, and hiatal hernia.
